laws.rule: Drivers may not read or view a text message, or type by hand on a hand-held phone or other mobile device, for any purpose while driving, except to call for medical or other emergency help (NMSA 66-7-374).

Watercraft registered outside New Mexico, and boats re-entering the state, must be inspected for aquatic invasive species (pest mussels and plants carried on boats) and decontaminated if needed before launching. Stopping is compulsory at any inspection station that is open, boats must be drained (plug pulled) while carried on New Mexico roads, and a watercraft 26 feet (about 8 m) or longer needs 14 days' notice to the Department before it is brought in. Knowingly transporting aquatic invasive species into or within the state is unlawful.

items.text: Adults 21 and over may buy, at one time, up to 2 ounces (about 57 g) of cannabis, 16 g of concentrate and 800 mg of edibles, and carry no more than that in public. More may be kept at home if it is out of public view. Using cannabis while driving or in public places such as restaurants, parks and footpaths is illegal, including at festivals and at dispensaries without a consumption lounge licence; use is limited to homes and licensed lounges. A public-use citation can bring a fine of up to US$50 (about A$71 at RBA 30 Oct 2026, A$1 = USD 0.7040).

Patients enrolled in another US state's, territory's or Washington DC's medical cannabis program, or a New Mexico tribal program, can buy as reciprocal participants. They register at a participating dispensary on their first purchase and show government proof of enrolment and a government ID from the same state every time they buy. Not every dispensary takes reciprocal patients. As of March 2026, patients from Alabama and Louisiana were not eligible because those states don't issue cards.

The Medical Psilocybin Act (Senate Bill 219, signed April 2025, in force 20 June 2025) sets up a state-regulated program for the medical use of psilocybin, the active compound in some mushrooms, run by the Department of Health. Conditions named include treatment-resistant major depression, PTSD, substance use disorders and end-of-life care. The Act requires the program to be running by 31 December 2027; one Department of Health page gives 31 December 2026. A nine-member Medical Psilocybin Advisory Board was still meeting in October 2026 and rules were being written, so there was no patient access yet.

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Treat a Pueblo as someone's home. Call the Tribal office first: access can close for private ceremonies, and some Pueblos charge entry. Most require a permit to photograph, sketch or paint, some ban photography outright, and cameras can be confiscated. Alcohol and drugs are strictly prohibited on Pueblos. Enter homes only by invitation; tipping a feast-day host is not appropriate. Taos Pueblo asks visitors to treat the village as they would their own home.
culture-and-protocol.sacred_or_restricted_places: Dances are religious ceremonies: silence is mandatory, with no questions, interviews, walking across the dance plaza or applause. Kivas, ceremonial rooms and cemeteries are for Pueblo members only. Don't climb walls or buildings. Obey OFF LIMITS signs. Taos Pueblo also asks visitors to obey Restricted Area signs, not to enter homes that are not marked as businesses, and not to enter the cemetery (which includes the old church ruins) or the river, the community's drinking-water source. Unexpected closures can happen for religious activities or a death in the community.

culture-and-protocol.photography_and_story_permissions: Taos Pueblo (Taos Pueblo Tourism): a camera fee of US$6 a person is listed on its photography page (about A$8.52 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026, A$1 = US$0.7040). Ask before photographing community members. Photography is not allowed in San Geronimo Chapel. Professional and commercial photographers, and artists who want to sketch or paint, must apply for pre-approval; fees vary. Sky City (Acoma Pueblo): cameras are not permitted during feast days or Christmas events; call 800-747-0181 (9 am to 5 pm) about other days, as the page lists no camera fee or permit.

layers.process: Admission listed on its visiting page: adults US$25; seniors, students aged 11 and up with ID, groups of 8 or more adults and military US$22 each; children 10 and under free (about A$35.51 and A$31.25 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026, A$1 = US$0.7040). The photography page lists a separate US$6 camera fee a person (about A$8.52). An earlier site page showed US$16 for adults, so confirm by phone (575-758-1028). Open 9 am to 4 pm daily; check the events calendar.

The site says Taos Pueblo closes to visitors for several weeks in late winter or early spring, and the length differs between its pages (six to ten weeks), so dates are not fixed. It also closes without notice for religious activities or a death in the community, and its events calendar lists an annual closure to all visitors on 20 to 31 August 2026. Call to confirm before travelling.
Professional and commercial photographers, and artists who want to sketch or paint, apply for pre-approval; fees vary. Contact Taos Pueblo Tourism, 575-758-1028.
